Issued at 320 PM CST Fri Nov 20 2026

REST OF THIS AFTERNOON - THIS WEEKEND:

There has been a slight uptick in precipitation amounts for this
weekend, though snowfall amount forecasts have not changed
substantially. 

We are starting to see the coverage in light rain showers fill 
in this afternoon in an area of isentropic ascent north of a 
warm front. Most of the coverage is in north-central and 
northeast Minnesota, as should also be the case much of this 
evening. However, this light shower activity shifts slightly 
east into the I-35 corridor, Arrowhead, and portions of 
northwest Wisconsin later this evening and tonight before seeing
a reduction in coverage late tonight into early Saturday 
morning as the surface low tracks into northwestern Ontario.

Another wave of light rain develops along and ahead of a west-
to-east moving cold front Saturday morning in the I-35 corridor
into northwest Wisconsin with rain shower activity continuing 
throughout the day in northwest Wisconsin before shifting into 
north-central Wisconsin for Saturday evening and night. 
Frontogenesis along this front will be maximized Saturday
evening and night, which will favor the highest rainfall
accumulations in north-central Wisconsin before the
precipitation associated with the cold front exits by early
Sunday morning. 

Rainfall and liquid-equivalent precipitation amounts remain
fairly light, though have increased over the last 12-24 hours. 
There is now a 40 to 70% chance for at least one-quarter inch of
rain in the Minnesota Arrowhead. Meanwhile, there is a 50 to 
90% chance for totals of at least one-quarter inch in northwest
Wisconsin, mainly along and east of a line from Spooner to 
Ironwood. The deterministic forecast rainfall amounts for these
regions is currently 0.15-0.40", with lesser amounts elsewhere.
Given the frontogenetic forcing along the cold front in north- 
central Wisconsin Saturday evening and night, higher total
rainfall amounts in the 0.50-0.75" range cannot be ruled out
(30-60% chances).

Colder air wrapping around on the back side of the departing 
low-pressure system Saturday night into Sunday will combine with
cold-advection and additional shortwave troughing aloft to 
produce scattered, light showers. This shower activity should 
gradually transition from rain to a rain/snow mix to light snow 
throughout Sunday from northwest to southeast. This snow ends 
for most of the area by Sunday night, but light lake-effect snow
is forecast to linger into Monday morning for the South Shore 
lake-effect snowbelts before drier air moves in. While not a 
locked-in scenario, the combination of steep low-level lapse 
rates, a small amount of MLCAPE (25-50 J/kg), and 20-25 mph 
northwest winds could produce snow squall potential (20-30% 
chance) Sunday afternoon into early evening for north-central 
Minnesota into the Arrowhead. Some hindering factors to travel 
impacts from these snow showers would be above freezing air and 
road temperatures, with highs in the mid-30s for much of the 
afternoon as well as lighter snowfall rates/accumulations. 
However, accumulations on roadways could have better potential 
to stick after sunset as air temperatures drop below freezing. 
Trends in snow squall potential will need to be watched closely.
As of now, the main impact would be brief, rapid reductions in 
visibility as any snow showers pass over a given location.

Snow accumulation with this system continues to look light and 
relegated mainly to the Iron Range into the Arrowhead and areas
north, as well as parts of the South Shore lake-effect
snowbelts. The probability for 1 inch or more of snow in those 
locations is 30-50%, with locally higher probabilities of 50-70% in
the higher terrain of Iron County. Probabilities drop off
quickly for 2"+ amounts, with a 20-40% chance in the higher
terrain of Iron County and little to no chances elsewhere.

As for temperatures the rest of today into this weekend, expect
well-above average high temperatures and low temperatures for 
this afternoon into Saturday. Some daily record warm
temperatures could be set today and record warm lows on
Saturday. See the Climate section below for details. Cooler,
more seasonably normal air moves into the Northland on Sunday
behind the cold front.

NEXT WORK WEEK:

Cooler, more normal temperatures for late November and a 
primarily drier pattern sets up for much of next work week as 
high pressure moves through the Upper Midwest and Great Lakes. 
Expect high temperatures in the upper 20s to mid 30s on Monday
to moderate slightly to the 30s for mid to late week. Lows will
largely be in the teens to 20s, with a 20-30% chance for upper-
single digits in the typical cold spots Monday night. Some 
troughing aloft on the backside of the high pressure Tuesday 
night into Wednesday could still bring very light snow chances
